stances.claim: Institutional response to CJ's two prior columns has been broad and prompt: CJ Peralta's chief of staff Ralph Jerome Salvador texted same-day that the Oct. 4 piece would be added to the agenda of the SC Committee on Revision of the Rules on Criminal Procedure (chaired by CJ Peralta); Justice Secretary Menardo I. Guevarra texted the next day that 'You hit the nail right on its head' and plans further consultations with the SC; Sandiganbayan Justice Maryann E. Corpus-Mañalac confirmed reforms would reduce court congestion; and Naga RTC Judge Soliman M. Santos Jr. did 'one better' by lengthily quoting CJ's column in his Oct. 5 People v. Orcine decision acquitting an accused detained without bail for nearly four years.

Compañero Romulo Macalintal exemplifies CJ's 2006 'Liberty and Prosperity' vision for the legal profession -- 'competent and ethical lawyers who are responsible, dependable, morally upright, and who courageously uphold truth and justice above everything else' -- because his guiding principle has always been 'to handle only meritorious cases,' a maxim he 'passed on to two of (his) children who... are also members of the bar.'

The late-1990s blank-check episode -- a losing Metro Manila mayor handing Macalintal a blank check for an election protest, Macalintal honestly telling him 'his case would not prosper' and returning the check -- concretely demonstrates the meritorious-case principle in operation.

Macalintal's declination of GMA-offered posts (Comelec chair, solicitor general) -- 'I did not have the management ability and experience at that time to handle these offices,' and 'I maintained only a strict client-attorney relationship with her... Honesty is always the best policy' -- further illustrates the ethical-lawyer model by showing that ambition discipline is part of professional integrity.

Macalintal v. Teh (Oct. 16, 1997) and its nine-year clemency-pursuit aftermath model the second face of ethical lawyering: after the SC ousted the judge for 'gross ignorance of the law' and forfeited his retirement benefits in response to Macalintal's appeal, Macalintal pleaded for clemency citing similar cases of lighter penalties; on January 31, 2005 the SC granted clemency, finding the judge 'sincerely repented... reformed his ways... renewed his life' -- and the friendship culminated in Macalintal becoming principal wedding sponsor of one of the judge's daughters.
stances.rhetorical_move: second-face-of-ethics narrative (win the case, then advocate clemency)

notable_anecdotes: Justice Secretary Guevarra's text the day after CJ's Oct. 4 column -- preserved with the Tagalog code-switching intact: 'Alam ninyo po, matagal na rin po naming pinag-uusapan ang issue na yan sa National Prosecution Service. You hit the nail right on its head. I intend to do further consultations... with the Supreme Court. Babalitaan ko po kayo.' -- the cabinet secretary's text-message register makes the institutional uptake personal.

Naga RTC Judge Soliman M. Santos Jr.'s Oct. 5, 2020 People v. Orcine decision quoting CJ's column 'lengthily' to acquit an accused 'who had been detained without bail for nearly four years' -- the same-week judicial uptake that materializes CJ's policy proposal in an actual acquittal.

The CJ Peralta chief-of-staff Salvador text -- same-morning, with concrete commitment to agenda the column in the SC Committee on the Revision of the Rules on Criminal Procedure -- making the institutional escalation traceable to a single text.

The Macalintal blank-check anecdote -- a losing Metro Manila mayor handing him a blank check, Macalintal returning it with the honest assessment that the protest 'would not prosper' -- the meritorious-cases principle made tangible in a single transaction.

Macalintal v. Teh's nine-year clemency journey -- Macalintal patiently pleading clemency for the very judge he had succeeded in ousting, citing similar suspension/fine cases, until the SC on January 31, 2005 (during CJ's incumbency) granted relief -- modeling the rare lawyer-pursues-clemency-for-former-opponent posture.

Macalintal closing the loop: he eventually became 'principal wedding sponsor of one of (the judge's) daughters' -- the most striking reconciliation arc in the column, from courtroom adversary to family friend.

CJ's 2006 'Liberty and Prosperity' back-cover vision quoted in full ('competent and ethical lawyers who are responsible, dependable, morally upright, and who courageously uphold truth and justice above everything else') -- using his own prior book as the standard against which Macalintal is measured.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reports the 'encouraging' institutional reactions to his prior two columns -- Oct. 4 on prosecutorial reform ('humbly proposed' guidelines to deter 'filing frivolous, reckless, malevolent, and politically-motivated charges') and Sept. 27 on SC short-shrifting facially baseless petitions ('differentiate shysters... from trustworthy lawyers'). On Oct. 4 itself, Compañero Ralph Jerome Salvador, chief of staff of CJ Diosdado M. Peralta, texted that the piece would be included on the agenda of the SC's Committee on the Revision of the Rules on Criminal Procedure, which CJ Peralta chairs. The next day, Justice Secretary Menardo I. Guevarra texted in code-switched Tagalog/English: 'Alam ninyo po, matagal na rin po naming pinag-uusapan ang issue na yan sa National Prosecution Service. You hit the nail right on its head. I intend to do further consultations... with the Supreme Court. Babalitaan ko po kayo.' Sandiganbayan Justice Maryann E. Corpus-Mañalac also texted that the suggested reforms would reduce court congestion and let magistrates focus on pending litigations. Naga RTC Judge Soliman M. Santos Jr. did 'one better' by quoting CJ's Oct. 4 column at length in his October 5, 2020 People v. Orcine decision acquitting an accused 'who had been detained without bail for nearly four years.' CJ hopes 'the huge chasm between probable cause and proof beyond reasonable doubt will soon be bridged and quality justice more speedily rendered.' Pivoting to the Sept. 27 column, he recalls his 'vision for the legal profession' from the back cover of his 2006 'Liberty and Prosperity' book: 'competent and ethical lawyers who are responsible, dependable, morally upright, and who courageously uphold truth and justice above everything else.' Compañero Romulo Macalintal embodies that vision: his guiding principle is 'to handle only meritorious cases,' a maxim he 'passed on to two of (his) children who... are also members of the bar.' In the late 1990s, a Metro Manila mayor who lost his reelection bid handed Macalintal a blank check as professional fee for an election protest; Macalintal honestly told him his case 'would not prosper' and returned the check. As GMA's lawyer he was offered Comelec chair and solicitor general but declined -- 'I did not have the management ability and experience at that time to handle these offices' -- and maintained 'a strict client-attorney relationship... Honesty is always the best policy.' The column closes with Macalintal v. Teh (October 16, 1997): after a judge fined Macalintal P100,000 for filing an inhibition motion alleging bias, Macalintal appealed and the SC ousted the judge and forfeited his retirement benefits for 'gross ignorance of the law.' Finding the penalty too harsh, Macalintal pleaded clemency for the judge over nine years, citing similar cases where respondents were merely suspended or fined; on January 31, 2005, the Court (with CJ already as CJ) granted clemency, allowing accrued leaves (but not full retirement), finding the judge 'sincerely repented for his transgression, reformed his ways, and renewed his life.' Macalintal recalls: 'I thought I would never meet the judge again. But one day, I received an invitation to attend his 75th birthday... We became good friends until his death some years back. I even became a principal wedding sponsor of one of (his) daughters.'
